The Gambler is a short novel from 1867 set in a decadent European casino town. It chronicles the descent of Alexei, a poor tutor caught in obsessive gambling and a volatile love affair with the imperious Polina. Through the perspective of escalating desperation and illusory hope, Dostoevsky portrays gambling as a psychological disorder, a substitute for authentic feeling and will that consumes the self. Alexei is a weak man of ambition without agency, drawn into the orbit of a wealthy Russian family and Polina, who tests his devotion through cruelty and demand. His gambling is not calculation but compulsion, an attempt to transcend his powerlessness and win Polina's love through sudden fortune. It is a fantasy of willful transformation. Polina sends him to the casino to win large sums to free her from debt. His wins and losses become a mirror of his emotional state: inflated hope, devastating shame. The setting is a fashionable spa-town casino, inspired by Wiesbaden, where wealthy Russians waste fortunes and moral standards corrode under perpetual temptation. Dostoevsky wrote the novella under financial pressure and partly from personal experience with gambling addiction. Its urgency is autobiographical. The protagonist's voice becomes increasingly fragmented and manic as compulsion deepens, rendering the psychological texture of obsession with devastating clarity. Through Alexei's obsession, Dostoevsky explores gambling as a secular substitute for faith and meaning, and compulsion as the replacement of authentic will with compulsive repetition.
